title: Five blessings of walking
hook: stamina for travel, for effort, good health, good digestion, lasting concentration

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn: standing, intending, turning. Your line was the turn counts too. Which in-between moment did you catch? Day one hundred and twenty.

Some families have a tradition: after the big dinner, everyone goes for a slow walk around the block. Nobody calls it medicine. It's just what you do. You feel better, your stomach settles, the conversation gets easier. It turns out the Buddha had his own list of reasons to walk, and one of them would make a grandmother nod. There's a short discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the numbered collection, in the book of fives. It lists five blessings of walking meditation. And they're wonderfully practical.
screen: `A SLOW WALK AFTER DINNER.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT MEDICINE.` → `FIVE BLESSINGS OF WALKING.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the Cankama Sutta, the walking discourse, AN 5.29. Here are the five. One: you can endure long journeys. In the texts, the Buddha and his monks travel on foot from town to town, and this is stamina for that road. Two: you can endure striving. The effort of practice, the long hours of sitting, the steady work of the path, all come easier to a body used to walking. Three: you're healthy. Four: what you eat and drink is well digested. That's the one the grandmother likes. Five: the concentration you gain while walking lasts a long time. The last one is worth slowing down for. The discourse simply says it lasts a long time. One way teachers explain it: concentration built while sitting perfectly still can scatter the moment you stand up. But concentration built while moving, feet lifting, placing, the body turning, is already used to movement, so it may hold up better when you get on with your day. Notice what this list is. There's nothing hidden or otherworldly in it. It's a teacher telling his students, in plain terms: this is good for your body, good for your practice, and good for the rest of your life. The Pali texts speak about the body in more than one way; elsewhere they ask monks to reflect on its impermanence and unattractiveness. But here, it isn't something to escape or despise. It's the vehicle for the path, and walking keeps it in working order. Today's practice fits the fourth blessing exactly: a slow walk after a meal. Not for steps on a tracker. Just to let the body settle. Walking steadies.
screen: `STAMINA FOR THE ROAD.` · `STAMINA FOR THE EFFORT.` · `HEALTH, AND GOOD DIGESTION.` · `CONCENTRATION THAT LASTS.` · then, large: `WALKING STEADIES.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly on your few paces of floor. Feel the whole body walking: the feet, the legs, the belly, the breath. Let the pace be relaxed, a little slower than normal. There's no labeling today unless you want it. Just walking, with attention, as if you'd just finished a good meal and had nowhere to be. At each turn, stand for a breath. If you're seated, feel the body breathing and the feet on the floor. The bell holds the time.
Samadhi. Concentration, collectedness: the fifth blessing of walking meditation, the kind that lasts long after you stop.
Your line: walking steadies. Today, after one meal, take a slow walk, even five minutes, and feel the body settle. Day one hundred and twenty.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners who do walking meditation sometimes walk after meals, and teachers cite the five benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya's walking discourse.

trapdoor: what you thought: walking is good exercise.
what it means: walking practice supports the body, the effort of the path, and a steadiness that lasts into the day.
what a scholar hears: AN 5.29, the Cankama Sutta, lists the five benefits; here the body's health is a support for practice, though other suttas ask monks to reflect on the body's unattractiveness.

notes: The five benefits are paraphrased from AN 5.29; confirm order and wording.

The explanation that walking-built concentration 'holds up better' when you move is a teacher's interpretation of the fifth benefit (the sutta says only that it lasts long); now framed as 'one way many teachers explain it'. Confirm framing.
Softened the claim that the Pali texts generally treat the body as the vehicle of practice; the texts also teach reflection on the body's unattractiveness (asubha). Keeper to confirm balance.
